title: Correcting gauge mid-project
subtitle: What to do when you realise your gauge is off after several rows
excerpt: Discovering a gauge problem after ten rows is different from discovering it on the swatch. The decision to continue or restart depends on the project type, how far off the gauge is, and how much the size matters.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book.

glossaryTerms.definition: The number of stitches and rows that fit in a measured area, usually 10 cm. Used to confirm the finished piece will come out the right size.
The difference between a body measurement and the corresponding finished garment measurement. Positive ease means the garment is larger than the body.

content.text: problem after starting a project requires a decision: stop and restart or carry on. The right choice depends on how far off the gauge is and what the project is. A few stitches per 10 cm off is tolerable in a non-fitted item; the same difference on a fitted garment produces something that does not fit.
Lay the piece flat without stretching. Do not measure at the cast-on or bound-off edge; the tension there is less reliable.
Measure 10 cm from the centre of the fabric, away from the edges. Pin at each end of the 10 cm span.
Count the stitches and rows between the pins. Compare to the pattern's gauge.
Non-fitted items (blankets, scarves, dishcloths): a gauge difference of 1 or 2 stitches per 10 cm usually does not matter. The piece will be slightly larger or smaller, which is tolerable.

Fitted garments (sweaters, hats with a specific head circumference, socks): even 1 stitch per 10 cm off can mean a size difference of several centimetres at full garment width. Restart is usually the right call.
. If the pattern is worked with generous positive ease and your gauge makes it a size larger, it may still fit.
When you continue with the wrong gauge

If you continue on the wrong gauge, recalculate the stitch counts for any shaping. If your gauge is 15 stitches per 10 cm where the pattern assumed 14, adjust the required stitch counts for each section using your actual gauge, not the pattern's gauge. See the pattern sizing guide for the method.

items.symptom: Gauge is tighter in the body rows than in the swatch
items.cause: Tension changed once the project had several inches of fabric below the working row.
items.fix: Many makers tighten slightly when the work feels heavier. Go up half a hook size and see whether the gauge stabilises after a few more rows.

items.symptom: Gauge matched the swatch but the piece looks stretched laterally
items.cause: The stitch count in a key row was higher than stated, adding extra width.
items.fix: Count the stitches in the current row. If it is over the stated count, find where the extra stitches appeared and frog back to that row.

content.text: Before restarting, work three extra rows on the mismatched piece using the corrected hook size. Check whether the gauge has stabilised to the correct number. Sometimes the tension self-corrects as the hook adjustment settles, and a full restart is not needed.
